narrative:
The model assessed your likelihood of failing the final year at 19%, which exceeds the 10% threshold that triggers the requirement to take remedial courses. While this may feel discouraging, understanding what shaped this prediction can help you move forward.

The three factors that most influenced the prediction all actually worked in your favor, pushing toward passing rather than failing — yet their combined effect was not strong enough to bring your risk below the threshold.

The most influential factor was your reason for choosing this school: you selected it based on its reputation. Among students not required to take remedial courses, about 27% shared this same reason, so this is not unusual, and it slightly reduced your predicted risk. Your history of no past class failures also helped lower your predicted likelihood of failing — students not obliged to take remedial courses have an average of zero failures, just like you, which is a positive sign. Finally, your aspiration to pursue higher education contributed positively as well, reflecting motivation that the model recognized as a protective factor.

However, other aspects of your profile — such as your very high amount of free time after school and a higher-than-average number of absences (10, compared to an average of roughly 3 among passing students) — likely kept your overall risk elevated.

The good news is that your attitude and track record show real potential. You should use the remedial courses as an opportunity to strengthen your academic foundation, work on reducing absences, and consider channeling some of that free time into structured study.
